config.title: Multiple State Variables

intro.title: Multiple State Variables
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build an interactive Angular component that manages multiple pieces of state simultaneously, such as a user profile form with separate fields for name, email, and age. You'll learn how to declare and work with multiple component properties that can change over time, understanding how each state variable operates independently while contributing to the overall component behavior. The core programming concept focuses on managing multiple reactive data properties using Angular's change detection system and property binding. You'll use Angular component properties, string interpolation, event binding, and two-way data binding to create a dynamic user interface that responds to multiple state changes. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to organize and coordinate multiple state variables to build more complex, interactive Angular applications.
intro.usecase: Multiple state variables are essential in modern web applications where users interact with complex interfaces containing independent pieces of data. Shopping cart applications track item quantities, user preferences, and checkout progress simultaneously, while dashboard applications manage filter selections, chart data, and notification states independently. Social media platforms use multiple state variables to handle post content, comment visibility, like counts, and user authentication status all at once. Form applications require separate state management for field values, validation errors, loading states, and submission status to provide smooth user experiences.

objectives: Initialize multiple state variables within an Angular component using property declarations
Implement independent event handlers that update different state variables separately
Bind multiple state variables to template elements using Angular's interpolation syntax
Construct form controls that manipulate distinct state properties through user interactions
Configure two-way data binding to synchronize multiple input fields with their corresponding state variables
Apply conditional rendering techniques to display content based on multiple state variable values
Update multiple state variables simultaneously within a single method when business logic requires coordinated changes

steps.title: Import Angular Component
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the Component decorator from Angular core
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing a utility from a library
import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Component decorator is imported and available for creating Angular components
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're importing Component specifically from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the import statement to bring in Component from '@angular/core'. This will allow you to create Angular components.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a component class named MultipleStateComponent and add the @Component decorator with selector 'app-multiple-state' and template as an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator above the class declaration. The decorator needs a selector property for the HTML tag name and a template property for the component's HTML.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

// Add @Component decorator and class here
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class with the @Component decorator configured with selector and template properties
successCriteria: Component class named MultipleStateComponent is created with @Component decorator containing selector 'app-multiple-state' and template property
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you have both the @Component decorator with the required properties and the component class declaration.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the @Component decorator above your class declaration. The decorator should include both selector and template properties.

steps.title: Initialize the first state variable
steps.instruction: Add a counter property to the component class and initialize it to 0
steps.hint: In Angular components, properties are declared as class members. Add the property declaration inside the component class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have a counter property initialized to 0, demonstrating the first state variable in Angular
successCriteria: A counter property is declared in the component class and initialized to 0
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the counter property is initialized to 0 and is declared as a class member.
steps.feedbackWrong: The counter property should be declared inside the component class and initialized to the value 0. Remember that in Angular, component state is managed through class properties.

steps.title: Initialize the second state variable
steps.instruction: Add a name property to your component class and initialize it to an empty string.
steps.hint: Add another property declaration similar to your first state variable, but initialize it with an empty string ('').
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have a second state variable called name initialized to an empty string, allowing you to manage multiple independent pieces of state.
successCriteria: A name property is declared and initialized to an empty string ('').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the name property is initialized to an empty string ('').
steps.feedbackWrong: add a name property and initialize it with an empty string (''). This creates your second state variable.

steps.title: Initialize the third state variable
steps.instruction: Add a boolean property called isVisible and initialize it to true in your component class.
steps.hint: Add the property declaration after your existing counter and name properties. Boolean properties in TypeScript can be declared as 'propertyName: boolean = value;'
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have three state variables: counter (number), name (string), and isVisible (boolean).
successCriteria: The isVisible property is declared as a boolean and initialized to true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the isVisible property is declared as a boolean type and set to true.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a boolean property called isVisible and set its initial value to true. The syntax should be: isVisible: boolean = true;

steps.title: Create the increment method
steps.instruction: Add a method named 'increment' that increases the counter by 1
steps.hint: Define a method inside your component class that adds 1 to the counter property
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have an increment method that adds 1 to the counter
successCriteria: A method named 'increment' is defined that increments the counter property by 1
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your method increments the counter by exactly 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment method should add 1 to the counter property. Try defining a method that uses this.counter++.

steps.title: Create the name update method
steps.instruction: Add a method called 'updateName' that takes an event parameter and updates the name property with the event target's value.
steps.hint: Create a method that accepts an event parameter and sets this.name to event.target.value to handle input changes.
steps.expectedOutcome: A method named 'updateName' that takes an event parameter and assigns event.target.value to the name property
successCriteria: The updateName method is defined and properly updates the name property from the input event
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your method takes an event parameter and updates the name property with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The updateName method should accept an event parameter and set this.name = event.target.value to handle input changes.

steps.title: Create the visibility toggle method
steps.instruction: Add a method named toggleVisibility that switches the isVisible property between true and false.
steps.hint: Create a method that sets isVisible to the opposite of its current value using the ! operator.
steps.expectedOutcome: A toggleVisibility method is added that inverts the current value of isVisible.
successCriteria: A method named toggleVisibility exists that toggles the isVisible property between true and false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your method toggles the isVisible property by setting it to its opposite value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleVisibility method should set isVisible to the opposite of its current value using the ! operator.

steps.title: Add the component template structure
steps.instruction: Add a template property to the component that contains three div elements: one to display the counter value, one to display the name, and one that conditionally shows content based on isVisible
steps.hint: The template should use interpolation to display the counter and name values, and use *ngIf directive for conditional rendering of the third div
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a template that displays the counter value, name, and conditionally rendered content
successCriteria: Template property is added with three div elements using interpolation for counter and name, and *ngIf for conditional rendering
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your template includes divs for counter, name, and conditional content with the correct Angular directives.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template needs three div elements: one showing counter with interpolation, one showing name with interpolation, and one with *ngIf for conditional rendering.

steps.title: Add interactive controls and wire events
steps.instruction: Add a button with text 'Increment' that calls the increment method, an input field that binds to the name property with two-way binding, and a button with text 'Toggle Visibility' that calls the toggleVisibility method.
steps.hint: Use Angular event binding with (click) for buttons and two-way binding with [(ngModel)] for the input field to connect the UI elements to your component methods and properties.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of Angular template with event bindings
<button (click)="save()">Save</button>
<input [(ngModel)]="username" />
<button (click)="reset()">Reset</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Three interactive controls are added to the template: an increment button that calls the increment method when clicked, an input field with two-way binding to the name property, and a toggle button that calls the toggleVisibility method when clicked.
successCriteria: Template contains a button with (click)="increment()" event binding, an input with [(ngModel)]="name" two-way binding, and a button with (click)="toggleVisibility()" event binding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress! Make sure you have all three elements: an increment button with (click) binding, an input with [(ngModel)] binding for the name, and a toggle button with (click) binding.
steps.feedbackWrong: add three interactive elements to the template: a button that calls increment() on click, an input field with two-way binding to the name property using [(ngModel)], and a button that calls toggleVisibility() on click.
